evals.prompt: Define semiotics for interface design in 2-3 sentences. Distinguish signifier from signified and name the foundational models the skill draws on.
expected_elements: Defines semiotics as the analysis/design of multi-channel sign systems, not aesthetic taste
Signifier = the perceivable form (icon, color, shape, position, word); signified = the concept/state/action/judgment it points to
Names the models: Peirce (icon/index/symbol), Saussure (signifier/signified), Barthes (denotation/connotation/myth), Norman (affordance)
States the goal is coherent intended meaning so users do not have to infer

evals.prompt: Use Peirce, Saussure, Barthes, and Norman to analyze a warning badge that combines a triangle icon, yellow color, and the word 'Review'.
expected_elements: Classifies the triangle/icon channel via icon/index/symbol reasoning
Separates each signifier (triangle, yellow, the word) from its signified
Separates literal denotation (caution) from connotation/judgment (attention needed, possibly error)
Uses signifier/affordance language for the action expectation the badge creates
Checks whether all three channels point to the same intended state

evals.prompt: When should an abstract or unfamiliar icon be paired with text, and when can a symbol stand alone? Explain the tradeoff using the icon/index/symbol distinction.
expected_elements: Symbols are arbitrary conventions — efficient once learned, opaque before
Abstract/unfamiliar icons need text pairing until the convention is learned
Strong existing convention (or a clear iconic resemblance) can carry an icon alone
Names the tradeoff: discoverability/clarity for first-time users vs. fluency/density for experts

evals.prompt: A product team says users misread a dashboard because green means both 'revenue went up' and 'costs went up'. Diagnose the semiotic problem and prescribe the fix.
expected_elements: Identifies a denotation/connotation conflict — direction of change vs. business judgment
Explains that green connotes 'good' so a cost increase reads as positive
Notes color is already communicating whether intended or not
Recommends pairing color with text, icon, shape, or another sign channel (never color alone)
Frames the fix as preserving trust and reducing misread inference

evals.prompt: Audit a disabled button that only becomes pale gray but still has hover styling and sits in the primary-action position of a dialog. What is wrong and how should it be fixed?
expected_elements: Identifies a weak/conflicting anti-affordance — greying alone is too subtle
Notes hover styling and primary placement still signify actionability
Recommends a strong anti-affordance: remove interactive signifiers, change cursor, reduce perceived affordance
Notes color alone is not a sufficient state signal
Checks that text/icon/shape/state cues all agree the element is unavailable

evals.prompt: A teammate routes 'draft the exact wording for this disabled-button tooltip' and 'pick the hex value for the warning badge' to the semiotics skill. Are these in scope? Distinguish semiotics from microcopy, visual-design-foundations, a11y, and semantics.
expected_elements: Neither is in scope: wording is microcopy, the hex value is visual-design-foundations/a11y
Semiotics owns the sign-system reasoning (what the sign should communicate), not the words or the craft values
a11y owns contrast/non-color-alternative compliance; semantics owns single-identifier meaning encoding
Offers the in-scope part: whether the chosen signs coherently signal 'unavailable' / 'warning'

evals.prompt: A designer says icon confusion is just subjective taste and users will learn the icon over time. Correct the misconception.
expected_elements: Rejects 'sign-system failures are merely taste' — every element communicates whether intended or not
Explains ambiguous icons impose inference cost and erode trust (sign drift compounds)
Notes only a few icons are widely recognized without labels; icon polysemy is the most common failure
Recommends text pairing, convention alignment, or testing rather than assuming meaning emerges automatically

evals.prompt: What would you check to verify a surface's sign system is coherent after applying this skill?
expected_elements: No signifier points to multiple unintended signifieds within the same system context
Important meanings are not encoded through color alone
Interactive vs. non-interactive states have distinct affordance signals
Icon metaphors are coherent, learnable, and consistent across surfaces
Direction (denotation) and judgment (connotation) are separated in metric/financial UI
Code-facing signs (function/variable/endpoint names) are not vague signifier failures
